issues.legal_issue: A claimant relying on a genealogy to establish succession must prove every link necessary to connect the claimant to the person whose estate is claimed.
material_facts: The claim to the estate depended on establishing a line of descent through several ancestors.
The claimant’s descent from one ancestor was accepted, but the evidence did not establish the necessary connections between that ancestor and the line of the former estate holder.
The Supreme Court found the documentary and oral evidence insufficient to prove the missing links.
issues.conclusion: The claimant did not prove the genealogy necessary to establish that he was the nearest reversioner, and the claim to title failed.
issues.legal_principle: In a succession or title claim founded on a genealogy, the claimant bears the initial burden of proving every necessary link; a missing link means the genealogy is not established. The Court assessed the evidence under the Evidence Act, including section 32(5), and the principles on pedigree evidence in Bahadur Singh v. Mohan Singh, Pershad Chowdhry v. Rani Radha Chowdharain, Abdul Ghafur v. Hussain Bibi, Mewa Singh v. Basant Singh, and Bhojraj v. Sita Ram.

predicates.inheritance_title_proceeding: A person seeks title to or succession to an estate on the basis of inheritance.
predicates.claim_depends_on_genealogy: The claimant relies on a chain of family relationships to connect themself to the former estate holder.
predicates.necessary_genealogical_link_unproved: The evidence does not establish at least one relationship necessary to complete the claimed chain of descent.

issues.definition: When an inheritance title claim depends on a genealogy and a necessary link in that genealogy is unproved, the claimant is not established as the nearest reversioner.

issues.legal_issue: An entry made by a public officer in an official record in the discharge of official duties may be admissible even if its evidentiary weight is slight or nil.
material_facts: The disputed report was an entry in a register held in a government collectorate.
A government officer prepared it in response to an official direction to investigate possession of lands.
The report referred to persons through whom the claimant asserted title, making it relevant to a fact in issue.
The report did not disclose the source of its information or how the officer verified the genealogical statements.
issues.conclusion: The report was admissible under section 35 of the Evidence Act, but its lack of disclosed sources and verification left it with insignificant probative value and no assistance in proving the claimed title.
issues.legal_principle: Section 35 of the Evidence Act requires an entry in a public or official book, register, or record, a statement of a fact in issue or relevant fact, and an entry made by a public servant in the discharge of official duties. Admissibility is distinct from probative value. The Court applied P.C. Purushothama Reddiar v. S. Perumal and considered Brij Mohan Singh v. Priya Brat Narain Singh in addressing the significance of the source of information.

rule.if: genealogy_title_proceeding and official_record_entry and entry_relates_to_relevant_fact and entry_made_in_official_duty

predicates.genealogy_title_proceeding: A title dispute requires proof of family descent through a genealogy.
predicates.official_record_entry: The evidence is an entry in a public or other official book, register, or record.
predicates.entry_relates_to_relevant_fact: The entry states a fact relevant to the dispute being tried.
predicates.entry_made_in_official_duty: A public servant made the entry while carrying out official duties.

issues.definition: In a genealogy-based title proceeding, an official entry relating to a relevant fact and made in official duty is admissible, while its weight depends on the reliability of its information.

issues.legal_issue: A judgment in personam that was not between the parties cannot generally prove the truth of its findings or recitals in a later dispute.
material_facts: The claimant relied on earlier judgments to support the asserted genealogy and title.
The parties to the present dispute had not been parties to those judgments.
The judgments were not judgments in rem, and the claimant sought to rely on their recitals and findings rather than merely their existence or operative effect.
issues.conclusion: The recitals and findings in the non-party judgments were inadmissible to prove the claimant’s genealogy or title.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 40 to 43 of the Evidence Act govern the relevance of judgments. A judgment in rem may be admissible beyond the parties to it, but a judgment in personam that is not inter partes is generally inadmissible to prove the truth of its findings, subject to limited purposes such as establishing the parties, decree, and property involved. Section 13 cannot be used to circumvent the specific rules governing judgments. The Court relied on John Cockrane v. Hurrosoondurri Debia, Jogendro Deb Roy Kut v. Funindro Deb Roy Kut, Gujju Lall v. Fatteh Lall, Maharaja Sir Kesho Prasad Singh Bahadur v. Bahuria Mt. Bhagjogna Kuer, and Coca-Cola Company of Canada Ltd. v. Pepsi-Cola Company of Canada Ltd.

rule.if: later_title_proceeding and prior_judgment_not_between_current_parties and prior_judgment_not_in_rem and recitals_offered_to_prove_truth

predicates.later_title_proceeding: A court is deciding a title or succession dispute after an earlier judgment was issued.
predicates.prior_judgment_not_between_current_parti: Neither side in the current dispute was a party to the earlier judgment.
predicates.prior_judgment_not_in_rem: The earlier judgment determined rights between particular persons rather than status or rights binding generally.
predicates.recitals_offered_to_prove_truth: A party offers the earlier judgment’s findings or recitals to establish the truth of the matters stated in it.

issues.definition: In a later title proceeding, findings in a judgment that was neither between the current parties nor in rem cannot be used to prove the truth of their recitals.

issues.legal_issue: Declarations or statements about pedigree made after a dispute has arisen are inadmissible as evidence of that pedigree.
material_facts: Some witnesses relied on family statements about the genealogy that were made after the succession dispute had arisen or proceedings had begun.
The statements were offered to prove the disputed family relationships.
issues.conclusion: Statements made after the controversy arose could not be relied on to prove the genealogy.
issues.legal_principle: Section 32(5) of the Evidence Act requires a statement about family relationship to have been made before the question in dispute was raised and by a person with special means of knowledge. The doctrine of post litem motam excludes statements made after an actual controversy or legal proceeding has begun. The Court relied on Kalka Prasad v. Mathura Prasad, Hari Baksh v. Babu Lal, Dolgobinda Paricha v. Nimai Charan Misra, and Kalidindi Venkata Subbaraju v. Chintalpati Subbaraju.

predicates.pedigree_evidence_proceeding: A party seeks to prove family relationships as part of a legal claim.
predicates.family_statement_offered: A party relies on a statement or declaration about family relationships.
predicates.statement_made_after_controversy_arose: The statement was made after an actual dispute over the subject had arisen or legal proceedings had begun.

issues.definition: When a family statement is offered to prove pedigree and was made after the controversy arose, it is inadmissible.

issues.legal_issue: Oral evidence of an ancient pedigree must be assessed for the witness’s special means of knowledge, source and circumstances of knowledge, interest, reliability, and corroboration.
material_facts: The witnesses sought to prove a long line of descent largely from information said to have been transmitted by relatives or other deceased persons.
Several witnesses did not identify a reliable source, occasion, or circumstances for their knowledge, and their accounts contained inconsistencies or memory problems.
The evidence did not provide substantial corroboration of the disputed links, and some statements were made after the dispute arose.
issues.conclusion: The oral evidence did not reliably prove the disputed genealogical links.
issues.legal_principle: Section 32(5) of the Evidence Act provides an exception for statements concerning family relationship when the declarant had special means of knowledge and the statement was made before the dispute arose. In evaluating oral pedigree evidence, the Court considered the witness’s connection to the family, the nature and source of the witness’s knowledge, the witness’s interest, the risk of post-dispute invention or imagination, and corroboration as time and memory permit. It relied on Bahadur Singh v. Mohan Singh, Pershad Chowdhry v. Rani Radha Chowdharain, Abdul Ghafur v. Hussain Bibi, Mewa Singh v. Basant Singh, and Bhojraj v. Sita Ram.

rule.if: pedigree_evidence_proceeding and oral_testimony_offered and (special_knowledge_source_unclear or testimony_unreliable or substantial_corroboration_absent or statement_made_after_controversy_arose)

predicates.pedigree_evidence_proceeding: A party seeks to prove family relationships as part of a legal claim.
predicates.oral_testimony_offered: A party relies on witnesses’ oral accounts to establish a genealogy.
predicates.special_knowledge_source_unclear: The witnesses do not clearly establish how, when, or in what circumstances they acquired their knowledge of the genealogy.
predicates.testimony_unreliable: The testimony contains material inconsistencies, weak memory, or other circumstances undermining its reliability.
predicates.substantial_corroboration_absent: The oral account lacks substantial corroboration appropriate to the age and subject of the asserted genealogy.
predicates.statement_made_after_controversy_arose: The relevant statement or account was made after an actual dispute over the subject had arisen or legal proceedings had begun.

issues.definition: In a pedigree proceeding, oral testimony is insufficient to prove disputed links when its knowledge source is unclear, it is unreliable, lacks substantial corroboration, or depends on statements made after the controversy arose.

issues.legal_issue: Dictionaries may be consulted to ascertain both the meaning of a word and its general usage when interpreting documentary language.
material_facts: The parties disputed the meaning of Persian words in an old report relied on to establish family relationships.
The Court examined the original wording and consulted standard dictionaries to assess the words’ meaning and usage.
issues.conclusion: The Court was entitled to consult dictionaries to determine the meaning and general use of the disputed words.
issues.legal_principle: Dictionaries may be used as an aid to ascertain not only the meaning of a word but also its general use. The Court relied on Coca-Cola Company of Canada Ltd. v. Pepsi-Cola Company of Canada Ltd.

predicates.document_interpretation_proceeding: A court must interpret words used in a document relevant to a dispute.
predicates.word_meaning_or_usage_disputed: The parties dispute the meaning or ordinary use of a word in the document.

issues.definition: When a court interprets a document and the meaning or use of a word is disputed, it may consult a dictionary.

issues.legal_issue: A state cannot obtain an escheat determination merely because the claimant before the court fails to establish entitlement to the estate.
material_facts: The states opposed the claimant’s asserted title but did not bring a properly constituted action claiming escheat on the basis that no heir existed.
The states had not given public notice inviting any potential claimant to come forward.
The failure of the claimant’s proof did not establish that no other heir existed anywhere.
issues.conclusion: The Court left the escheat plea undecided, held that the status quo should continue, and left the states to establish any claim of escheat in a properly constituted action.
issues.legal_principle: The burden lies heavily on a government asserting escheat to prove the absence of any heir. Courts generally disfavor escheat unless its essential conditions are fully established, and public notice must be given so that potential claimants may come forward. Failure of one claimant’s case does not by itself establish that no heir exists.

rule.if: estate_title_proceeding and state_relies_on_escheat and claimant_failure_only and public_notice_not_given

predicates.estate_title_proceeding: A court is deciding competing claims to an estate.
predicates.state_relies_on_escheat: A state asserts that the estate should pass to it because no heir is entitled to it.
predicates.claimant_failure_only: The state relies on the current claimant’s failure to prove title without establishing that no other heir exists.
predicates.public_notice_not_given: The state has not given public notice inviting potential heirs to come forward.

issues.definition: When a state relies on escheat in an estate title proceeding but shows only the current claimant’s failure and has not given public notice, the escheat claim is not determined on that record.
